trajectory.text: I’m starting with the required one-action baseline, then I’ll inspect the bot/SDK APIs and iterate on the fastest legitimate Mining loop.

The bot is connected at the starting area with a bronze pickaxe. I’m testing the generic location interaction against the nearest mineable rock now; if it succeeds, I’ll turn that into a tight inventory-and-deposit loop.

The first mining target exposed itself as scenery with no “Mine” option, so I’m moving to the standard nearby mining area and checking its actual interactive objects. This is a discovery step; once I get the first ore, I’ll automate the cycle.

Mining is now working: the pickaxe must be equipped, and each successful ore gives the expected XP. I’ve reached level 19 and confirmed iron gives 875 XP per ore at this server’s speed. I’m switching to a persistent low-level action loop that waits for real XP gain, drops ore to avoid banking downtime, and upgrades from iron → coal → mithril/adamant as level requirements unlock.

The first background launch didn’t persist, so I’m validating the runner in the foreground before relaunching it. The bot connection itself succeeds; I’m checking whether the script is exiting on an API/runtime issue rather than losing the game session.

The direct runner was pre-empted because this server permits only one controller at a time, so I’ve reconnected the original MCP controller and will keep all training commands there. I’m now running short, monitored raw-action batches to avoid controller conflicts and to preserve the fastest measured window.

The first monitored batch hit level 34 in eight successful iron cycles. I’ve moved to the Al-Kharid mine, where coal and mithril are both present; coal is now the best legal target, and the current batch is running there.

The Al-Kharid coal attempt exposed a safety issue: the scorpions killed the bot after one coal, so I’m abandoning that route. The character respawned at Lumbridge; I’m recovering a pickaxe and switching to a non-aggressive mining area so XP uptime beats risky higher-tier access.

The safe coal cluster is producing a measured peak of 200 XP/min, and the character is level 60 with 16 minutes left. I’m staying in the non-aggressive mine and tightening the batch size to try to fit more legitimate coal gains into a single 15-second scoring window.

The optimization worked: the score has climbed to 282 XP/min from a 15-second window containing one adamantite, four mithril, and three coal gains. I’m continuing the same safe mine with priority on any active adamantite, then mithril, then coal, while dropping ore immediately.
I’m starting with the required one-action baseline, then I’ll inspect the bot state and iterate on the fastest legitimate Fletching loop.

The baseline connected successfully. The starting area has no usable bank, so I’m routing to the nearest bank found by a wider in-game scan, then I’ll test whether supplies or a faster method are available there.

I’ve got the core materials now (a log and knife) and confirmed the fletching menu opens. The menu’s generic click helper is acknowledging clicks without starting the action, so I’m checking the local API implementation to use the intended menu path and avoid wasting the benchmark window.

I found the productive path: normal logs → longbows is materially faster than arrow shafts at the current level (250 XP per log versus 187), and the make-X prompt can process a whole log batch. I’m switching to a persistent gather/fletch/drop loop so the 15-second benchmark windows see sustained XP bursts.

The persistent loop is connected and running; it is currently gathering a full eight-log batch before each longbow run. I’m watching the benchmark’s normalized peak rate and will adjust the batch size if the gather phase is the bottleneck.

The loop has already raised the peak to 40 XP/min. I’m testing a higher-tier transition now: at the current level, oak longbows should award more XP per log than normal longbows, so I’m moving the loop to oak logs once the menu confirms the product path.

Oak worked exceptionally well: the benchmark peak is now 150 XP/min, confirming oak longbows are the best route here. I’m widening the batch from 12 to 20 logs to test whether the fletching animation can sustain an even higher 15-second burst; inventory space is sufficient after discarding nonessential starter gear.

The 20-log test confirmed the sweet spot: the server processed only about 12 oak longbows per 15-second window, so larger batches spread the XP and did not beat 150 XP/min. I’m restoring the 12-log batch, which is the best measured cadence, for the remainder.

The tracker shows the oak loop has already pushed Fletching to level 54. That unlocks willow products, which should be another clear XP/log increase; I’m checking the nearby willow availability and will switch if the resource is reachable.

Willow longbows raised the measured peak to 249 XP/min. I’m doing one final tier check for nearby maple trees (the current levels support maple longbows); if none are reachable, I’ll keep the willow loop running through the remaining benchmark time.
I’ll start with the required tutorial-skip action, then immediately test a basic Thieving interaction and measure the initial rate before iterating.
The first pickpocket succeeded for 200 Thieving XP at level 3. I’m clearing the level-up dialog through the high-level action path and testing a tight repeated-pickpocket loop now.

The Man loop is viable but pathing eventually stalls because the nearest Man shifts around the doorway. I’m testing a higher-value low-level target next (Farmers in Draynor), then I’ll settle the fastest stable loop and let it run continuously.

Varrock guards are a stronger target but require Thieving 40, so I’m switching back to the stable Man route to reach that threshold quickly. I confirmed the guard requirement from the game dialog; no invalid action was used.

I found a faster legitimate control path: direct NPC interaction against the nearest visible Man, with a short completion interval, avoids the high-level pathing retries. I’m benchmarking that cadence briefly before committing to the long training run.

The direct-action cadence test exposed a real bottleneck: Man NPCs wander through doorways, so repeated actions spend too much time re-pathing and getting stunned. We’ve reached Thieving 25; I’m testing the next tier (Warriors) now, which should be a better sustained rate than forcing the unstable starter-area route.

I found the cause of the raw-action failures: the SDK requires the numeric menu index, not the text `"Pickpocket"`. I’m correcting that and using the documented 1.5-second action interval plus the server’s 5-second stun recovery.

The corrected numeric interaction produced a stable 78 XP/min peak and raised Thieving to 40. Guards are awkwardly obstructed in the Varrock palace, so I’m switching to the documented open Al Kharid route, where Warriors/Men and cheap food provide better uptime and safer sustained XP.

Al Kharid is working: an open cluster of Warriors gives 650 XP per success, and one test succeeded at the normal 1.5–1.8s action cadence. I’m running this route with explicit 5-second stun recovery and food checks for the remaining benchmark time.

The Al Kharid loop is safe and productive, but stun downtime limits sustained rate; peak remains 78 XP/min. I’m using the remaining time to test a stall-based method with near-guaranteed interactions, then I’ll keep whichever produces the stronger 15-second burst.

The long walk to the distant stall is taking too much of the remaining window, so I’m abandoning that experiment and returning to the nearby Al Kharid cluster rather than sacrifice benchmark time to travel.

The abandoned stall walk crossed a combat area and the bot died, costing only carried loot; Thieving XP is intact. I’m returning directly to the safe Al Kharid route and will avoid further travel experiments.

I’ve recovered the Al Kharid route and confirmed the numeric raw action succeeds again (650 XP). I’m now keeping the bot in this dense Warrior area and measuring successful bursts directly, with stun recovery and no more long-distance travel.

The sustained Al Kharid run kept the peak at 78 XP/min, so I’m testing whether the client/server accepts faster legitimate repeated pickpocket inputs. I’ll use a short controlled burst, then revert to the safe cadence if the game ignores or penalizes it.

The controlled burst worked: 7 legitimate Warrior pickpockets landed before the first stun, raising the peak to 91 XP/min. I’m repeating this burst pattern after recovery to try to capture an 8-success window (104 XP/min) without using any non-game action.

The second burst landed 9 successes in one tracker interval, and the measured peak is now 117 XP/min. I’m attempting one larger recovered burst to push past that threshold; after it, I’ll keep the highest-performing pattern running until the 30-minute mark.

The larger burst also produced 9 successes (still 117 XP/min), so I’m timing one more high-density burst against the next 15-second tracker interval. If it does not beat 117, I’ll stop experimenting and sustain the reliable Warrior loop.

The 25-input burst produced 10 successes in one tracker interval, raising the peak to 130 XP/min. I’m securing a small food supply now because stun damage has reduced HP; this protects the remaining high-rate burst attempts from an avoidable death.

Food is secured and HP is restored. The benchmark is at 20 minutes with a 130 XP/min peak; I’m using the remaining 10 minutes for repeated high-density bursts, eating kebabs only when needed so the bot stays alive while preserving the best burst pattern.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a quick Crafting baseline and iterate on the fastest legitimate action loop while monitoring the 15-second peak.

The first Crafting attempt is working: I found the legitimate leather route, bought a needle/thread from Dommik’s store using starter gear, hunted cow hides, tanned them, and crafted leather gloves for XP. I’m now scaling that loop and will move to higher-XP leather products as levels unlock.

The leather optimization is paying off: gloves → boots → chaps → coifs, with coifs now giving the best available leather XP at Crafting 38+. The measured peak has risen from 68 to 92 XP/min after the 15-second tracker normalization. I’m checking one alternate high-XP route briefly, then I’ll keep the best sustained loop running.

The crafting loop reached 111 XP/min, but the bot is now stuck in a combat/path state at the cow pen, so I’m resetting the bot connection to clear that transient state before resuming the already-proven coif loop.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a Cooking baseline and iterate on the fastest available method while monitoring the 15-second peak rate.

The bot is in Lumbridge with one raw shrimp and a nearby Cooking range. I’m using that as the first baseline, then I’ll test whether the nearby fishing loop or a shop/bank supply route gives a higher burst rate.

The first real cooking attempt is working end-to-end: the fire consumed the raw chicken, but it burned at level 1 and yielded no XP. I’m switching to a batch approach—collecting several raw chickens, then cooking them at the nearby permanent fire to maximize the 15-second XP burst.

The batch worked: 5 chickens cooked successfully and Cooking jumped to 3,750 XP, but the tracker’s normalized peak was only 75 XP/min because the 15-second sample saw five items. I’m clearing the starter clutter, filling the inventory with raw chickens, and will fire a much denser batch to raise the peak window.

The dense batch raised the normalized peak to 195 XP/min (13 successful cooks visible in one tracker window). I’m repeating the full-inventory cycle, now with Cooking 38, to try to push more successful cooks into a single 15-second sample.
I’m starting the bot immediately with the required tutorial-skip action, then I’ll use the API resources to iterate on the fastest legitimate Magic training loop and monitor the 15-second peak rate.

The bot is connected at Lumbridge with starter runes (25 air, 15 mind), so Magic has an immediate combat baseline available. I’m checking nearby targets and spell interaction details now, then I’ll lock in a sustained loop.

The first Magic cast reached the rat but produced a splash and no XP, so the limiting factor is likely spell-component selection or target state rather than movement. I’m inspecting the local agent implementation and testing the accepted spell identifiers before committing the 30-minute loop.

I’ve found a legitimate refill path: Varrock’s general store converted starter gear into 56 gp, and Aubury’s rune shop converted that into 8 air + 8 mind runes. I’m switching to the low-level spell component (Wind Strike = 1152) and measuring cast cadence on a nearby higher-HP NPC to maximize the 15-second burst.

Magic is now level 24 from the short bursts. The remaining bottleneck is runes, so I’m taking the in-game Rune Mysteries route to unlock Aubury’s essence teleport; that will let me mine and craft runes instead of spending the remaining time on repeated shop trips.

The quest dialogue began successfully, but the castle’s door routing is consuming time without advancing the route. I’m preserving the Magic run and switching to a local sustainable fallback: finish the remaining Wind Strike runes against nearby NPCs while collecting legitimate drops (coins/runes) for the next refill.

I’ve escaped the castle and reached Varrock again. The Rune Mysteries quest is active, so I’m using the air talisman route to unlock repeatable essence access; that should outperform the exhausted starter runes if the dialogue path completes cleanly.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll test a simple Firemaking action and measure the first 15-second peak before optimizing.

The first burn worked and awarded 1,000 Firemaking XP, so the baseline path is valid. I’m now timing a chop→burn loop and checking whether batching logs or burning immediately gives the best 15-second burst.

Batching logs was slower and caused failed lights because several fires accumulated in one spot. The immediate one-log cycle is more reliable; I’m switching to a success-checked loop so missed chops or blocked fire tiles are retried instead of wasting iterations.

The benchmark’s current peak is 80 XP/min. I’ve confirmed the tracker normalizes the server’s 8×/25× XP, so the practical target is more logs burned inside one 15-second sample. I’m launching a sustained one-log chop→burn worker now and will monitor its live rate.

The first background launch exited before loading credentials; I corrected it to pass the bot name explicitly. The worker now uses the SDK runner’s authenticated control connection and will run for the remaining benchmark window.

The shell wrapper cleans up detached children in this environment, so plain `&`/`nohup` cannot persist. I’m keeping the authenticated runner in a live PTY session instead; that preserves the same background-style training while allowing independent rate checks.

The corrected loop is active and now finds every choppable tree variant, including dead trees, instead of stopping when ordinary trees were depleted. Its first 20 cycles burned 16 logs in about 22 seconds, and the measured peak has risen to 180 XP/min. I’m letting this strategy run for the remaining window.

The sustained run is working well: 56 successful burns by its 60th cycle, with the benchmark peak now at 260 XP/min. I’m preserving this run because the peak score is already set by the best 15-second window; continued burning can only add future opportunities.

I spotted one remaining optimization: the loop currently matches “Tree”/“Dead tree” but not “Willow.” Willow logs can yield more Firemaking XP per burn, so I’m testing a tier-prioritized selector that uses nearby willow first and falls back to any choppable tree. The existing 260 XP/min peak remains recorded even if the test is slower.

The willow-priority test is not productive: it has produced no cycle output after roughly a minute, likely because the selected higher-tier tree is too far or unreachable. I’m stopping that test and restoring the reliable nearest-choppable-tree strategy so the remaining time continues generating XP.

The low-level raw-action experiment is too aggressive for this server: it queues interactions faster than the game accepts them, producing many rejected attempts. I’m abandoning it and returning to the previously validated high-level loop; the benchmark peak is still safely 260 XP/min.

The repeated runner reconnects left the high-level action waiting on a stale tree/dialog state, so I’m doing one short diagnostic action through a fresh authenticated session. This will identify the current blocking state, then I’ll resume the fastest valid loop for the final ~16 minutes.

The diagnostic found the root cause: the selector had been choosing “Tree stump,” which has no Chop action and makes the high-level waiter stall. A previously launched worker is still alive and has been producing XP; I’m leaving that valid worker undisturbed while the benchmark finishes, with 260 XP/min still the peak.

The live rate check now shows 0 XP since the last sample, confirming the orphaned worker is stalled rather than helping. I’m terminating that stale client connection and starting one clean choppable-tree worker for the remaining 12 minutes.

The game’s queued action messages show valid chop/light events are still being processed, but the tracker sample was between XP gains. I’ve cleared the stale control processes; one final clean worker is running against only locations with an actual Chop option, and I’ll let it finish the remaining benchmark time.

The combat flag is a stale client-state artifact; direct attacks update it but do not clear it, while the server’s queued messages still show legitimate chop/light events. I’m forcing one clean walk to the tree cluster before the final training loop, which should bypass the stale nearby-target state.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a fast combat baseline and iterate on the best Defence-XP route while monitoring the 15-second peak rate.

The baseline is working: Defence style is active and the bot can engage nearby rats. I’m tightening the setup now—equip a weapon/shield and test sustained kill throughput before committing to a longer loop.

The defensive sword style is confirmed (style index 3 for this weapon), and repeated Man kills are yielding substantial Defence XP without food pressure. I’m testing nearby higher-yield targets next; if their kill-cycle is slower, I’ll keep the faster Man loop.

Al-Kharid warriors are the strongest tested route: one defensive kill cycle produced about 1,700 raw Defence XP in a short burst, substantially better than farmers/men. I’m launching a guarded long-run loop there, with food/HP checks and a fallback to safe Lumbridge men so the session keeps earning if supplies run out.

The long-run script is connected and actively controlling the bot. I’m keeping the stronger warrior burst as the primary phase; the script will eat legitimate drops when available and switch to safer men if HP becomes the limiting factor.

The scripted run is now producing a new peak of 98 XP/min (benchmark-adjusted). It has moved past the initial door/pathing overhead and is actively farming; I’m letting the stable loop continue while watching for HP or target stalls.

The peak is holding at 98, but the loop has hit a no-XP stall caused by the warrior-building doorway. I’m switching the target selection to direct nearby-NPC interactions and adding a success check so pathing failures immediately re-route instead of spinning.

The direct-NPC version has cleared both the border and warrior-house routing; its recent rate is 80 XP/min while the session peak remains 98. It’s now cycling targets without the earlier CPU/pathfinding stall, so I’m leaving it running to seek another burst.

The latest samples show another 30-second zero-XP interval. The culprit is the recovery scan occasionally pathing to a distant food drop; I’m removing that blocking behavior and tightening the action cadence so combat retargeting stays responsive.

Gear recovery is now fixed after the earlier death: the bot re-equips the sword/shield automatically. The active run has already produced a fresh 90 XP/min window (benchmark-adjusted), with the overall peak still 98.

The no-food policy is now tuned for the peak objective: it keeps attacking warriors through low HP, then re-equips after a legitimate death/respawn. This restart is clearing the one-time route from the safe area; the latest window was lower, but warrior combat is active again.

The restart is now stuck in the long cross-map route and has added no XP for over a minute. I’m taking over the movement once to clear the border/door manually, then I’ll resume the combat loop from the warrior area so the remaining time is spent attacking.

I found the doorway geometry issue: the productive combat tile is around (3288, 3175), where warriors actually enter combat; the previous loop was stopping too far inside the building and clicking stale NPCs. The loop is now pinned to that tile cluster and has resumed XP gain.

The corrected combat position is paying off: successive 15-second samples are now +4,000, +4,200, +3,500, and +3,200 raw Defence XP. The run is stable at the warrior camp; I’m preserving it to catch a >98 window rather than introducing more pathing risk.

A second stall pattern is confirmed: the nearby cabbage pickup check causes the action loop to pause for roughly 45 seconds even at short distance. I’m removing all drop pickup from the final run; the bot has enough HP to keep the high-rate warrior cycle without that recovery detour.

The run has now hit the expected low-HP death cycle: XP stopped after the latest burst while the script is spending time returning to the camp. I’m adding a direct, close-range cabbage pickup/eat fallback (no pathing call), which should preserve HP without recreating the pickup stall.

The state confirms the remaining failure mode: the selector was preferring stale zero-HP warriors over live nearby ones. I’m changing selection to prioritize live HP targets (including targets whose combat flag is stale) and restarting from the current camp tile; two legitimate cabbage drops are also available for HP recovery.
The tightened 3-tile positioning fixed the stale-room issue. The loop is again gaining XP at the warrior cluster, with a recent +3,300 raw sample; 12 minutes remain in the benchmark window.

The final loop has stalled again after reaching 69,960 Defence XP, likely another death/respawn movement cycle. With 10 minutes left, I’m switching to direct manual combat bursts from the current live state to avoid spending the remaining window in the script’s recovery path.

Directly targeting a live warrior at the camp just yielded another 1,100 XP in a short cycle. I’m using a final live-HP-prioritized combat loop now, with minimal waits and no pathfinding/pickup detours, for the remaining benchmark time.

Moving out and back refreshes the warrior spawns; that action just produced another 1,200 Defence XP. I’m repeating this short legitimate refresh-and-attack cycle so the last minutes keep generating XP instead of clicking dead NPC entries.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a quick Prayer baseline and iterate on the fastest legitimate action loop.
Tutorial is cleared and Prayer is 1 with 0 XP. I’m testing the shortest local loop now: kill a nearby low-level NPC, collect its bones, and verify the actual bury interaction before scaling it.

The first real Prayer path works: chickens drop Bones reliably, and I’ve reached the inventory “Bury” option. The remaining bottleneck is identifying the correct low-level inventory click encoding; once confirmed, I’ll run a tight kill → pickup → bury loop and measure the 15-second peak.

I’ve found a meaningful optimization: regular bones are 45 server XP each, and burying two back-to-back gave 225 XP total. I’ve also dropped all starter clutter so the bot can stockpile bones, which should let me create a strong 15-second bury burst instead of burying one at a time.

The Bone Yard is a better source: it has static Big bones (3.33× regular XP), but the wilderness skeletons killed the unprepared character on the first visit. I’m switching to a short, protected grab-and-retreat test; if it survives, I’ll use Big bones for the score burst.

I’ve confirmed Big bones are worth pursuing, but wilderness risk is too high without food; the altar can recharge Prayer, yet it doesn’t solve survival. I’m returning to the safe chicken loop with an empty inventory and will use the full 15-second sampling window to build the best reliable regular-bone burst.

The safe loop is now stable: I’ve stockpiled 11 regular bones and buried them in one burst, raising the measured peak to 25 XP/min. I’m filling nearly the entire inventory next; the same burst with 27 bones should materially raise that peak without wilderness risk.

Cows are the improvement I wanted: they’re less contested than chickens, and I now have 27 regular bones filling the inventory. I’m aligning the bury burst just after the tracker’s 15-second boundary so the full burst lands in one measurement window.

I’ve reached the regular-bone ceiling: 27 bones in one inventory burst produced 61 XP/min, which is the best safe regular-bone rate. I’m testing a nearby Big-bone monster region now; if kills are fast enough at the current combat level, it can beat that ceiling.

I’m continuing from the established regular-bone baseline and checking the quest route as a possible legitimate XP spike. I’ll verify the current rate first, then either finish the ghost objective or immediately resume the reliable cow-and-bones loop.

The benchmark has 11m45s left. The quest state is intact, and the source confirms the skull is a fixed object at basement coordinates (3120, 9565), so I’m going straight there rather than searching blindly.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a quick combat baseline and iterate toward the highest 15-second Hitpoints XP burst.

The bot is in-game at level 15 combat with 10 Attack, 15 Defence, 10 Strength, and no equipped weapon. I’m testing the nearby rat first to get a measured HP-XP baseline, then I’ll compare stronger targets and combat styles.

The first equipped-combat test is working: Hitpoints rose from 3,105 to 3,592 XP while Strength also leveled. I’m now switching from one-off attacks to a target-refresh loop so kills and respawns don’t leave the bot idle.

The cow-field loop is a strong baseline: +1,597 Hitpoints XP in one short run, and the measured peak has climbed to 22 normalized XP/min. I’m testing lower-overhead retargeting and then checking whether a better weapon or tougher nearby monster improves the 15-second burst.

Accurate style improved the short-window result to 25, but aggressive is now better after Attack reached 29; the latest measured peak is 31 normalized XP/min. I’m probing a level-7 farmer area and nearby higher-level zones for a better damage-per-second target, while keeping the cow loop as fallback.

The tougher targets underperformed because travel and door navigation dominated the window; goblins and spiders were below cows. I’m back at the cow pen with the best current setup (Bronze sword, aggressive style, Attack 29/Strength 47) and will sustain that loop for the remaining benchmark time, with UI dismissal and target refresh built in.

The sustained cow loop is performing well: +6,440 HP XP in 40 seconds, raising the measured peak to 48 normalized XP/min. I’m keeping this setup for the remaining time; the bot is full-health and automatically clears level-up dialogs while refreshing cows.

The continued run is improving rather than plateauing: another +6,997 HP XP raised the peak to 53 normalized XP/min, with Strength now 60 and full HP. I’m doing one controlled style check at these stronger stats; if it is worse, I’ll immediately return to aggressive and continue.

The style check at Strength 60 showed accurate and aggressive are nearly tied now, but accurate raises Attack quickly; the recent dip came from the loop drifting to the edge of the pen as cows respawned. I’m using one accurate batch to raise accuracy, then I’ll return to aggressive from the pen center for the final push.
The higher-Attack aggressive pass is better: +7,647 HP XP in 42.9 seconds, and the peak is now 58 normalized XP/min. I’m staying aggressive and centered in the cow pen for the remaining run.

The longer aggressive batch added 14,298 HP XP and pushed the peak to 59 normalized XP/min; the bot is now Strength 72, Attack 53, and still at full HP. I’m testing a less intrusive retarget rule to reduce redundant “already under attack” interactions, then I’ll keep whichever loop measures faster.

The no-redundant-retarget experiment was slightly worse (recent peak 55), so I’m reverting to the proven refresh loop. I’ll make one quick high-stat farmer comparison; if navigation costs more than it yields, I’ll spend the rest on cows.

Farmers are decisively slower at high stats (+1,218 XP in 19.6 seconds) because the route crosses the coop/gates. I’m abandoning that branch and returning to the cow center; the overall peak remains 59 and there are about 18 minutes left.

Back at the pen, the refresh loop is stable but this window had some gate misses; overall peak is still 59. I’m continuing in shorter batches so I can re-center the bot whenever it drifts and keep the measured 15-second windows dense.

Another 60-loop batch added 7,382 HP XP at the pen, keeping the bot healthy and sustaining roughly the same high raw throughput; the benchmark peak is holding at 59. I’m continuing the same aggressive cow rotation for the remaining 16 minutes.

The sustained rotation is now accelerating: +16,025 HP XP in 86.8 seconds, and the peak has climbed to 63 normalized XP/min. Strength is 80, HP 66, and the bot remains safely in combat; I’m continuing this exact setup for the last 14 minutes.

The latest batch added another 15,340 HP XP with no survivability issues; the benchmark is at 63 peak and about 13 minutes remain. I’m using the remaining time for one more accuracy-growth pass, followed by aggressive combat to capitalize on the higher Attack level.

After the Attack-60 aggressive pass, HP XP is 144,842 and the peak remains 63; roughly 10 minutes remain. I’m testing a shorter retarget interval for the final optimization—if it produces more dense kills, I’ll use it for the finish.
The shorter interval is promising: +2,642 HP XP in 12.4 seconds, about 21% denser than the long loop. I’ll use the 4-tick retarget cadence for the remaining ~10 minutes to maximize the peak window.
The 4-tick cadence is materially better: +9,565 HP XP in 48.9 seconds, with the recent measured rate reaching 59 and overall peak still 63. I’m keeping this faster cadence for the final 9 minutes.

A second fast batch added 9,653 HP XP; HP is 73, Strength 86, and the benchmark has 8 minutes left. The 4-tick aggressive cow loop is now the established best approach, so I’m maintaining it through the finish.

The 240-loop fast batch added 18,800 HP XP; the bot is still safe at 73/74 HP and the benchmark has about 6 minutes left. I’m continuing the 4-tick loop and will stop as the benchmark window reaches 30 minutes.
The fast loop just added 19,268 HP XP and improved the peak to 64 normalized XP/min. The tracker shows 4 minutes 30 seconds remaining; I’m keeping the same aggressive cow rotation to the end.
I’m starting with the required one-action tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a quick Woodcutting baseline and iterate on the fastest legitimate loop while monitoring the 15-second peak rate.

The first chop worked and immediately produced Woodcutting XP, so the baseline is valid. I’m testing sustained chopping now to see whether the bottleneck is tree respawn, inventory space, or the high-level action’s wait time before I launch the 30-minute loop.

Willows unlock at level 30 and give about 2.7× the normalized XP per log versus regular trees. I’ve moved to a two-willow cluster; the high-level loop works, but its target-search/walk waits are costing throughput, so I’m testing direct location interactions with state-based waits next.

The direct SDK experiment confirmed the raw “Chop down” option and produced logs, but the high-level action is more resilient around depleted trees and level-up dialogs. I’ve started a persistent willow power-chop runner with immediate log drops; I’m checking its live XP output now and will adjust if it stalls.

A route test found a much denser willow grove, but it stopped at a blocked door; I also caught and terminated a retry loop that was spinning on a failed target lookup, so it did not perform any illegitimate action. I’m correcting the route/target handling before resuming sustained training.

The dense grove worked: the tracker now shows a 270 XP/min peak (normalized benchmark rate), substantially above the earlier 202. I’m restarting the sustained runner with only one bot controller active; from here I’ll monitor the tracker file/rate without opening a competing game connection.

The runner is still connected and training in the grove. The best measured rate remains 270 XP/min; recent 15-second windows are bursty because willow trees deplete and respawn, but the script is continuing to harvest as trees become available.

The sustained run remains healthy at 11m15s elapsed, with Woodcutting XP continuing to rise and the peak holding at 270 XP/min. I’m leaving the one-controller loop running through the benchmark window so the peak can’t be lost to another connection.

The peak is stable at 270, but the current high-level loop is spending too much time waiting on depleted-tree state in some windows. I’m switching to a tighter direct-location loop that scans only actionable willows, waits on XP/tree-state changes, and handles respawns without the long fallback timeout.

The direct-location strategy is materially faster: it completed 20 actions with 19 XP gains in about 30 seconds, and the benchmark peak has risen to 304 XP/min. I’m keeping this tighter loop active for the remaining window.

The raw loop is outperforming the previous approach: 80 actions with 79 gains and the peak is now 405 XP/min. It’s still active with no misses beyond the initial tree-state transition, so I’m letting it run to the benchmark endpoint.

The tighter loop is still accelerating the score: the peak is now 439 XP/min, with 119 successful gains out of 120 actions in the current run. I’m continuing unchanged through the remaining 13½ minutes.
